Paper_name: Perceiving the Self and Emotions with an Anxious Mind: Evidence from an Implicit Perceptual Task
Summary: This study investigated perceptual biases to emotional and self-related stimuli in individuals with sub-clinical anxiety compared to healthy controls. Using a self-emotional shape-label matching task, the researchers found that anxious participants exhibited a diminished perceptual self-bias. Furthermore, the severity of anxiety was correlated with an emotional bias towards valenced other-related stimuli. The results confirm altered self-prioritization in anxiety and link anxiety severity to altered responses to emotional others. These findings could have implications for the early diagnosis and treatment of anxiety disorders.
Author: Michella Feldborg, Naomi A. Lee, Kalai Hung, Kaiping Peng, Jie Sui
Journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
Conclusion: The main results demonstrate that individuals with sub-clinical anxiety show a reduced self-prioritization effect compared to healthy controls. Anxiety severity was also associated with a bias towards emotionally valenced stimuli related to others. This confirms the hypothesis of altered self-perception and emotional processing in anxiety, suggesting these perceptual biases could be relevant for understanding and treating anxiety disorders.
